headline: From Zhejiang EE Student to China's Most Consequential AI Bet
lede: A 4chan-style greentext recently made the rounds on X, narrating in bullet-point shorthand how an electrical-engineering graduate from Hangzhou became the man behind DeepSeek. The joke lands because the biography is real, and the punchline is geopolitical.
body:
Liang Wenfeng was born in 1985 in Wuchuan, a county-level city in Guangdong Province, to two primary-school teachers — a background that perhaps explains his later preference for institutions built around curiosity rather than prestige. He studied electronic information engineering at Zhejiang University, earning a bachelor's in 2007 and a master's in 2010, with a thesis on object-tracking algorithms for low-cost cameras. It is a minor historical irony that a man who would eventually stockpile ten thousand of the world's most advanced AI chips began his academic career optimising code for cheap hardware.

In February 2016, Liang and two Zhejiang classmates incorporated High-Flyer (*幻方*, or "magic square"), a Hangzhou-based *quantitative hedge fund* — one that uses mathematical models and algorithms, rather than human judgment, to execute trades. The firm grew quickly. By August 2021 it had crossed one hundred billion yuan (approximately $14 billion at the time) in assets under management, earning it a place among China's so-called "Four Kings of Quant-Investing." That same month, having decided the fund was becoming too large for its own alpha, it stopped accepting new subscriptions — a rare act of self-restraint in an industry not known for turning away money.

What High-Flyer was doing with the proceeds was more unusual still. Beginning in 2020, Liang had started building GPU clusters under a project he called Fire-Flyer. By 2021, Fire-Flyer II was operational: ten thousand Nvidia A100 chips, costing roughly one billion yuan, humming away in a Hangzhou data centre at an avowed utilisation rate of ninety-six percent. Liang has said the entire A100 stockpile was assembled before Washington tightened its semiconductor export controls on China in October 2022 — a detail that transformed what looked like an eccentric side project into a strategic asset of considerable national significance. The chips he bought casually are now ones his competitors cannot acquire at any price.

In April 2023, Liang announced that High-Flyer would spin out a dedicated artificial-intelligence research body. By July of that year, DeepSeek was incorporated as an independent company, with High-Flyer as its principal backer and Liang personally holding just one percent of the equity. The stated ambition was not to build another application layer on top of Western foundation models, but to pursue *AGI* (artificial general intelligence — the speculative point at which AI systems match or exceed human cognitive performance across domains) from first principles. "Someone must step onto the frontier," Liang told an interviewer. "For years, Chinese companies have been accustomed to leveraging innovations developed elsewhere. This time, our goal isn't quick profits but advancing the technological frontier."

The greentext that circulated on X compresses this arc into comic bullet-points — the EE student who teams up with "cracked classmates," the quant firm that casually outgrows its own alpha, the GPU hoard assembled just before the export ban slammed shut. What the format captures, perhaps better than a conventional profile, is the contingency of the whole story: that DeepSeek's computing substrate was bought with trading profits, that those profits funded chips that America then banned, and that the models trained on those chips went on to rattle global markets in January 2025. Liang kept a copy of the Chinese edition of *The Man Who Solved the Market* — the biography of *Renaissance Technologies* founder Jim Simons — and wrote its preface. On the eve of DeepSeek-R1's release, he posted that preface to his WeChat Moments. The parallel he was drawing was not subtle, and it was not wrong.

concepts.definition: A 4chan storytelling convention: first-person anecdotes written in bullet-point fragments preceded by '>', typically used to compress biographical or autobiographical narratives into deadpan comedy.
An investment vehicle that uses mathematical models, statistical analysis, and algorithms to generate trading signals, rather than relying on discretionary human judgment.

Artificial general intelligence — the theoretical threshold at which AI systems can match or exceed human cognitive performance across a broad range of tasks, as opposed to narrow AI trained for specific domains.
The secretive US quantitative hedge fund founded by mathematician Jim Simons, widely considered the most successful trading firm in history, and an explicit inspiration for Liang Wenfeng.

books.title: The Man Who Solved the Market
books.author: Gregory Zuckerman
books.relevance: Biography of Jim Simons and Renaissance Technologies; Liang Wenfeng wrote the preface to the Chinese edition and cited it as a formative influence.
